title: Storing food
summary: Store food so it keeps: somewhere cool, dry and dark. Below 85°F (29°C) is best, and never above or beside the stove, under the sink or in a damp garage or basement. Keep it covered, in tightly closed glass, metal or heavy food-grade plastic. Date everything, put new food behind old and use the oldest first. The date on most food is about quality, not safety. Throw away food that pests got into.

list: Somewhere cool and dry (USDA), and dark if possible (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet; New York State Department of Health).

Temperatures below 85°F (29°C) are best. Over 100°F (38°C) harms canned food, and the risk of spoilage jumps as the temperature rises (USDA). University of Illinois Extension says to keep canned food between 50°F and 70°F (10°C and 21°C).
Never above or beside the stove, under the sink, in a damp garage or basement, or anywhere exposed to high or low temperature extremes (USDA).
Not in a basement that is prone to flooding (New York State Department of Health).
Away from sunlight, damp spots, and vents, pipes or furnaces that make the temperature swing (University of Illinois Extension).
Off the floor, in a clean, dry, dark place away from any source of moisture (University of Georgia Extension).
In a small home: bedroom or coat closets, under beds or behind furniture (Oregon State University Extension).

blocks.p: Keep canned food where it won’t freeze: never store it anywhere exposed to high or low temperature extremes (USDA). From Protect an unheated house, word for word: “A can that froze may swell. Never use a swollen can: throw it out (USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service).” “Throw out frozen cans that thawed at 40°F (4°C) or warmer, even if they are not swollen. Cans that thawed and froze again are not safe (USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service).”

list: Keep food covered at all times (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet), sealed in containers with tight-fitting lids (CDC).
Store boxed food in tightly closed plastic or metal containers (Ready.gov).
Use only food-grade containers made for storing food: harmful chemicals can leach into food from containers not meant for it (Oregon State University Extension).

Good choices: airtight plastic food storage containers, glass jars with screw-top lids, or metal cans that are not rusty (University of Georgia Extension). Glass breaks: pack jars with cardboard strips or crumpled newspaper between them (Oregon State University Extension).
Open boxes and packages carefully, so you can close them tightly after each use (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet; University of Illinois Extension).

Put opened sugar, flour, dried fruit and nuts into airtight jars or cans. Wrap cookies and crackers in plastic bags and keep them in tight containers (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet; University of Illinois Extension).

Rice, instant cereal, potatoes or dry milk that is not in its own package with cooking directions: write the directions or mix ratios on a card and keep it with the food (University of Georgia Extension).
Before you buy, check that packages are sealed and unbroken, with no holes (University of Minnesota Extension).
Store food in tightly closed glass, metal or heavy plastic containers, or in the fridge or freezer (University of Minnesota Extension).
Keep storage areas clean, and clean up crumbs and spilled food right away (University of Minnesota Extension).
Check stored food for insects, rodents and water damage every six months (Oregon State University Extension).
Found food with insects in it? Throw it away. Then check all the other food they could get into: there may be more than one infested source (University of Minnesota Extension).

Older food you are not sure about: freezing it at 0°F (-18°C) for at least four days kills any eggs or insects (University of Minnesota Extension; University of Alaska Fairbanks Extension gives the temperature in °F).
Washing shelves with bleach, ammonia or detergent will not keep pantry insects from coming back, and the chemicals could be dangerous if they touch food (University of Minnesota Extension).

blocks.p: Rats and mice can spread disease and contaminate food (CDC). Keep food and water away from them (CDC). From Garbage and dirty water, word for word: “Don’t eat or drink anything rodents may have touched (CDC).” How to close holes, trap them and clean up droppings safely is in Garbage and dirty water; cleaning food surfaces afterwards is in Clean and disinfect.

sections.h: Date it and use the oldest first

list: Date everything with a marker when you buy it and when you open it (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet; University of Georgia Extension; University of Illinois Extension).
Put new food at the back and older food in front (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet).
Use what you store and replace it: rotate staples once or twice a year (University of Georgia Extension). Check your pantry every few weeks and use the canned food you have had for a while (USDA).
Food kept only for emergencies: label it as emergency food, keep it in its own place, and keep a list of dates when it needs checking (University of Georgia Extension).
Replace expired items, and rethink what you need every year as your family changes (Ready.gov).

blocks.p: USDA’s times for food kept on the shelf. Over several years canned food changes in taste and texture, and its nutritional value eventually drops (USDA).

head: Food
On the shelf, unopened
After opening, in the fridge
rows: Low-acid canned food: meat and poultry, stews, soups (not tomato), pasta products, potatoes, corn, carrots, spinach, beans, beets, peas, pumpkin
High-acid canned food: juices, tomatoes, grapefruit, pineapple, apples and apple products, mixed fruit, peaches, pears, plums, berries, pickles, sauerkraut, foods in vinegar-based sauces or dressings
Tuna and other seafood in pouches

blocks.p: For best quality, use canned food within one year (University of Georgia Extension). An older federal booklet gives these shorter times (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet):

list: Use within 6 months: boxed powdered milk; dried fruit and dry, crisp crackers in a metal container; potatoes.

Use within 1 year: canned condensed meat and vegetable soups; canned fruits, fruit juices and vegetables; ready-to-eat cereals and uncooked instant cereals in metal containers; peanut butter; jelly; hard candy and canned nuts; vitamin C.
Dried beans stored for more than three years may not rehydrate (Oregon State University Extension).
Freeze-dried foods may claim a 20- to 30-year storage life, but that does not ensure quality. Once opened, they spoil quickly in moist, humid air (Oregon State University Extension).
Except for infant formula, the dates on food are for quality, not safety, and federal law does not require them (USDA).
“Best if Used By” or “Best if Used Before”: when the food will be at its best flavor or quality. Not a purchase or safety date (USDA).
“Sell-By”: how long the store displays the food for sale. Not a safety date (USDA).
“Use-By”: the last date for use at peak quality. Not a safety date, except on infant formula (USDA).

blocks.warn: Never buy or use infant formula after its Use-By date (USDA).

blocks.p: Dates are not an indicator of the food’s safety (USDA). From Is it still good?, word for word: “Throw out any food with an unusual smell, color or texture; a normal one proves nothing: food that looks and smells normal can still make you sick (CDC). When in doubt, throw it out (CDC).”

list: Don’t buy bulging, rusted, leaking or deeply dented cans (USDA).

Check stored cans now and then for rust, leaks, bulges, bad dents and broken seals. A dent on a seam or on the end of the can can break the seal, and so can a large dent in the side, even if you can’t see it. Replace any can you find like this, and don’t eat from it (University of Georgia Extension).

blocks.p: Which cans and jars to throw out, and how to get rid of a suspect one, is in Is it still good? and Food poisoning and botulism.

list: Keep all food at 0°F (-18°C) or lower. Food kept constantly at 0°F is always safe; only its quality suffers with long storage, so freezer storage times are for quality only (USDA).
Keep an appliance thermometer in the freezer to check the temperature (USDA).
Wrap food well, and overwrap packages for long storage, to prevent freezer burn. Freezer burn does not make food unsafe, only dry in spots: cut those parts away before or after cooking (USDA).
Don’t freeze canned food or eggs in their shells (USDA).
